title: The rains retreat again

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sermon heard again, each truth with its own job, and the line: the wheel turns.

A monk has just promised to stay put for the whole rainy season. Then a message comes. A lay family who supports the monastery wants him to come and bless a new house, a few days' walk away. Or worse: his mother is ill. Does he go? Does the promise mean staying inside the monastery walls no matter what? The monks in the Buddha's time asked exactly this kind of question, and the answers are in the monastic rule. You've met the rains retreat before, and how it began with complaints about trampled crops. Today, look at the promise itself: what it holds, and where it bends.
screen: `A PROMISE TO STAY PUT.` → `THEN A MESSAGE COMES.` → `WHERE DOES IT BEND?`

segments.voice: First, the promise. At the start of the rains, each monk settles into one dwelling and declares that he will spend the rains retreat there. In Pali the season is vassa, the rains. It isn't a vow of silence or a lockdown. It's a vow of place. Then the bend. The monastic rule, in the section on entering the rains, allows a monk to leave on short business, up to seven days, and return. When? If he's sent for by a lay supporter who wants to give a gift or hear the teaching. If a fellow monk or nun is sick and needs help. If his mother or father is ill. The rule is careful: he goes, does what's needed, and comes back inside the time. So the retreat isn't a wall against people. It's a home base you return to. Why staying matters: wandering is good for meeting people; staying is good for going deep. In one place for a season, the same path to the same well, the same room, the same faces, there's less to plan and more room to practice. By custom, a monk's seniority is even counted in rains. Last, the lay side. In Theravada lands, some lay people take on a practice for the season too: keeping extra precepts on moon days, giving something up, or going to the temple more often. Not a season in a monastery; just one thing, kept in one place, all season long.
screen: `A VOW OF PLACE.` · `LEAVE FOR NEED, THEN RETURN.` · `STAYING LETS IT GO DEEP.` · then, large: `STAY IN ONE PLACE.`

segments.voice: Feel where you're sitting, the floor, the chair, the room around you: a place you could return to. Bring back the one practice you chose a few days ago and ask: could I keep this one thing for the season, here, not perfectly, just coming back the way a monk comes back inside the seven days? If it feels too big, make it smaller until it fits, and rest in the place itself.
The rains retreat. Vassa, the season when monks stay in one place, leaving only briefly for real need. Today's word.
Your line: stay in one place. A vow of place still bends for someone who needs you. Rain or shine, see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries monks enter the rains retreat after the Asalha full moon, each declaring a dwelling for the season; some lay people take on extra precepts or give something up for the same months.

chat.says: If a monk vows to stay put all rainy season, can he ever leave?
options: Yes, for real need, like a sick parent, for up to seven days, and then he returns.
No. Once the vow is made, he can't leave the walls until the rains end.
Yes, whenever he likes, since the vow only means keeping silent while there.
chat.meaning: The monastic rule lets a monk leave on short business, up to seven days, for a supporter, a sick monk or nun, or an ill parent, then return.

vassa.meaning: the rains, the monks' season of staying in one place
